463.title: Balak: only the word I'm given (Numbers 22:38)
463.hook: Balaam can speak only the word God puts in his mouth
463.tomorrow: Balak: how goodly are thy tents
463.howItsDone: Balaam's oracles are read in the portion of Balak each summer, and Jewish commentators, starting with Rashi, read his words alongside the question of what was really in his heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the donkey saw the angel three times before the famous seer saw anything. Your line was the donkey saw first. Whose quiet warning did you hear out? Day four hundred sixty-three.

You've been asked to give a toast, or write a reference, or say a few words at a meeting, and the person asking has made it very clear what they'd like you to say. Maybe they've even done you a favor. And the thing they want you to say isn't quite true. Balaam arrives in Moab in exactly that spot. King Balak meets him at the border, a little annoyed that he took so long, and promises him honor and reward. Everyone knows what the king is paying for. And Balaam's first words set the terms.
screen: `A TOAST, A REFERENCE, A FEW WORDS.` → `BALAK MEETS HIM AT THE BORDER.` → `BALAAM SETS THE TERMS.`

segments.voice: In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, Balaam says: "the word that God putteth in my mouth, that shall I speak." He'd already told Balak's messengers something like it: even if the king gave me his house full of silver and gold, I couldn't go beyond the word of God. Then comes something close to comedy. Balak takes him up to a high place, builds seven altars, and offers sacrifices. Balak is waiting for a curse. Balaam opens his mouth, and out comes this: "How shall I curse, whom God hath not cursed?" Balak is beside himself. I brought you here to curse my enemies, he says, and you've blessed them. So he tries a different hilltop, the top of Pisgah. Seven more altars. Maybe from a new angle, the curse will come. It doesn't. Balaam says, in paraphrase, God has blessed, and I cannot turn it back. Then a third place, Peor. Same result. Three hilltops, twenty-one altars, and not one curse. A new view doesn't change what's true. The rabbis didn't treat Balaam as a hero for this. Rashi notices that, of all the things to mention, he brings up silver and gold, and reads it as a man who wanted the money and simply couldn't get around the word. That's what makes the scene interesting. Even someone who'd rather say something else can find that the true word is the only one that comes out. In the story, whatever was in his heart, his mouth was held to what God gave him, and the curse that was bought and paid for turned into a blessing.
screen: `ONLY THE WORD GOD PUTS IN MY MOUTH.` · `HOW SHALL I CURSE?` · `THREE HILLTOPS, TWENTY-ONE ALTARS.` · `A NEW VIEW DOESN'T CHANGE THE TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say only what's true today. Settle, and breathe. Think about the conversations ahead of you today. Is there one where you might be tempted to say what someone wants to hear rather than what's so? A compliment you don't mean, a promise you can't keep, a yes that's really a no. Find the true sentence you could say instead, kind and plain. Hold it in your mind. You don't need to be harsh; you only need to be true. Breathe with it until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Balak. The king who moved his hired seer from hilltop to hilltop, hoping for a curse, and got only the word God gave.
Your line: only the true word. Today, before you say something to please someone, check it once: is this actually true? Day four hundred sixty-three.

464.title: Balak: how goodly are thy tents (Numbers 24:5)
464.hook: the curse becomes a blessing, and his words now open the morning service
464.howItsDone: Many Jews say Mah Tovu on entering the synagogue in the morning; in most prayer books it opens the morning service, followed by verses from the Psalms about coming into God's house.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three hilltops, twenty-one altars, and Balaam could speak only the word God put in his mouth. Your line was only the true word. Did you catch one pleasing thing that wasn't true? Day four hundred sixty-four.

Walk into almost any synagogue on a weekday morning, and the first words many people say as they come through the door are a line of Torah. It isn't from Moses, or David, or a prophet of Israel. It was first spoken by a foreign seer, hired by an enemy king, standing on a hill and trying to curse the people below. Balaam's third try, at Peor. He looks out over the camp of Israel, spread out tribe by tribe in the valley. And instead of a curse, these words come out.
screen: `THE FIRST WORDS AT THE DOOR.` → `SPOKEN BY A HIRED SEER.` → `THE THIRD TRY, AT PEOR.`

segments.voice: In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "How goodly are thy tents, O Jacob, Thy dwellings, O Israel!" In Hebrew, the first two words are Mah tovu: how good. What did he see that was so good? The Talmud, and Rashi after it, give a surprising answer. Balaam saw that the entrances of their tents didn't face one another. Nobody could look straight into a neighbor's home. Living close together, they still gave each other privacy. That's the goodness he saw: not grandeur, but decency between neighbors. The Talmud also gives Balaam's blessings a darker reading. Rabbi Yochanan said, in paraphrase, from the blessings of that wicked man you can learn what curses he meant to say. And the rabbis later read tents and dwellings as the houses of prayer and study, the places Israel would gather. Then came the prayer book. Mah Tovu became the opening of the morning service, the verse said on entering the synagogue, followed by lines from the Psalms about coming into God's house. Not everyone was comfortable starting the day with Balaam. A sixteenth-century rabbi, Solomon Luria, is reported to have begun from the second verse instead, because the first came from Balaam's mouth. Most prayer books kept it anyway. There's something fitting about that. Words that were bought to curse, said by someone who'd rather not have said them, became the first thing many Jews say every morning. The blessing outlived the man and the money.
screen: `MAH TOVU: HOW GOODLY ARE THY TENTS.` · `DOORS THAT DIDN'T FACE EACH OTHER.` · `THE OPENING OF THE MORNING SERVICE.` · `A CURSE THAT BECAME A FIRST WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say Mah Tovu entering a room. Settle, and breathe. Picture the next room you'll walk into: your kitchen, your office, a classroom, a friend's home. If you pray, you can say, as you cross the threshold, the line from Numbers: how goodly are thy tents, O Jacob, thy dwellings, O Israel. If you don't, simply pause in the doorway for one breath and look for one good thing about the place and the people in it. Practice it now in your mind, then breathe until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Mah Tovu. How good. Balaam's blessing over Israel's tents, now the first words of the morning service.
Your line: how goodly are thy tents. Today, notice one way the people you live or work with give each other room, and thank them for it. Day four hundred sixty-four.

465.title: Balak: dwelling alone (Numbers 23:9)
465.hook: Balaam sees "a people that shall dwell alone"
465.howItsDone: Balaam's first oracle is read in the portion of Balak in summer, and the phrase 'a people that dwells alone' is often quoted in Jewish discussions of identity and history.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mah Tovu: Balaam's blessing over tents whose doors didn't face each other, now said at the start of morning prayers. Your line was how goodly are thy tents. Did you pause in a doorway? Day four hundred sixty-five.

Remember being the only one at the table who didn't eat something, or the only kid who left early on Friday, or the one whose holidays fell on different days from everyone else's? Being different can feel like standing in a doorway while everyone else is already inside. Balaam's very first blessing, on the first hilltop, has a line about that. He looks down at Israel's camp from the top of the rocks, and he sees a people that doesn't blend in. He means it as a blessing.
screen: `THE ONLY ONE AT THE TABLE.` → `STANDING IN THE DOORWAY.` → `FROM THE TOP OF THE ROCKS.`

segments.voice: In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, Balaam says: "it is a people that shall dwell alone, And shall not be reckoned among the nations." In Hebrew, am levadad yishkon. A people that dwells by itself. Readers have heard this line in very different keys. Some hear a promise: a small people will keep its own shape through history, its own Sabbath, its own calendar, its own language of prayer, and won't simply dissolve into whatever empire is passing through. Others hear something heavier, an ache that runs through Jewish history, of being set apart whether you chose it or not. Both readings have been held by serious people, and the verse doesn't settle it. But here's a detail worth knowing. The same Hebrew root, badad, alone, shows up again at the very end of the Torah, in Moses' last blessing. There it sits right beside the word for safety: Israel dwells in safety, alone. In that verse, being alone isn't exile. It's security, like a house with its own walls. Some readers draw a difference from that pairing. Lonely means cut off. Alone, in this sense, means whole: having a center of your own, so you can sit at anyone's table without losing yourself. Balaam was hired to curse. Looking down from the rocks, he saw a people who didn't need to be like everyone else to be all right. And whether you hear it as gift or burden, the tradition kept the line, and still reads it aloud every summer.
screen: `AM LEVADAD YISHKON.` · `A PROMISE, OR AN ACHE.` · `BADAD BESIDE SAFETY.` · `ALONE MEANS WHOLE, NOT CUT OFF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: appreciate one way you're different. Settle, and breathe. Think of something about you that doesn't match the people around you: a practice you keep, a food you skip, a belief, an accent, a way you spend your weekends. Notice if it usually feels like a burden or something to explain. Now try holding it as a blessing for a moment: something that gives you a center of your own. You don't need to love it. Just let it be part of you. Breathe until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Balak. The portion where a hired seer looks down from the rocks and sees a people that shall dwell alone, and calls it a blessing.
Your line: alone isn't lonely. Today, when you're the only one doing something your way, notice it without apologizing for it. Day four hundred sixty-five.

466.title: Pinchas: a covenant of peace (Numbers 25:12)
466.hook: after violent zeal, a covenant of peace, and the word "peace" is written with a broken letter
466.howItsDone: In Torah scrolls the vav of shalom in Numbers 25:12 is written with a small break, and when the portion of Pinchas is read in summer, the broken letter is often pointed out and discussed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Balaam looked down from the rocks and blessed a people that dwells alone. Your line was alone isn't lonely. Did you let one difference stand without apology? Day four hundred sixty-six.

Balaam's blessings are over, and the story turns dark fast. At a place called Shittim, many Israelites are drawn into the worship of a local god, Baal of Peor. A plague breaks out in the camp. In the middle of the crisis, a leader from the tribe of Simeon brings a Midianite woman into his tent in full view of everyone. And Pinchas, the grandson of Aaron, takes a spear, follows them in, and kills them both. The plague stops. It's a hard scene to read. What God says next is a surprise.
screen: `THE STORY TURNS DARK AT SHITTIM.` → `PINCHAS TAKES A SPEAR.` → `WHAT GOD SAYS NEXT.`

segments.voice: A new portion opens, named for Pinchas. God says he turned back the divine anger, and then, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "Behold, I give unto him My covenant of peace." Peace. To the man who just killed two people. Then there's a detail you can only see in a Torah scroll. In the word shalom, peace, in this verse, the letter vav, the tall straight line in the middle, is written with a break in it. The Talmud mentions this broken vav, and Torah scribes still write it that way today. Nobody in the text explains it, so the commentators have offered readings. One line of interpretation says the break is a warning: peace that comes after violence, even violence the text approves of, is never whole. Something in the person who did it, or in the community, stays cracked. And the rabbis were careful about zeal in general. The Talmud says the law permitted what Pinchas did in that exact moment, but that if someone came to ask whether to do the same, they wouldn't be told yes. One way to read it: a zealot who stops to ask has already lost the certainty the act requires. In other words, the tradition honored Pinchas and, almost in the same breath, refused to turn him into a model anyone should copy. There's a word for passionate zeal in Hebrew, kin'ah, and the portion uses it of Pinchas. But the reward God gives him isn't more zeal. It's peace. As if to say: your fire stopped a plague; now carry the opposite of fire.
screen: `MY COVENANT OF PEACE.` · `THE BROKEN VAV IN SHALOM.` · `PERMITTED, BUT NOT TAUGHT.` · `ZEAL REWARDED WITH PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: temper zeal with peace. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you feel fiercely about, so fiercely that you've been sharp with someone over it. A cause, a value, a family rule. Let yourself feel how strong it is. Then picture that broken letter, a tall line with a small gap in it. Ask: where could a little peace go into this fire? A softer tone, a question instead of a verdict, an apology for how you said it. Hold that thought gently until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Pinchas. The zealous grandson of Aaron, given a covenant of peace, with peace written in the scroll with a broken letter.
Your line: peace is written broken. Today, when you feel a rush of righteous anger, let one breath of gentleness in before you act on it. Day four hundred sixty-six.

467.title: Pinchas: the five sisters (Numbers 27:1–11)
467.hook: Zelophehad's daughters ask to inherit; God tells Moses they speak right
467.tomorrow: Pinchas: a shepherd for the flock
467.howItsDone: The daughters of Zelophehad are read in the portion of Pinchas each summer, and their names, Mahlah, Noa, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah, are named in full each time the story is read.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pinchas, the zealot, was given a covenant of peace, and the word peace is written in the scroll with a broken letter. Your line was peace is written broken. Did you soften one fire? Day four hundred sixty-seven.

A rule that has always been the rule, and it leaves someone out. It's easy to grumble about a rule like that at the kitchen table and leave it there. The people are counted again, family by family, to divide the land they're about to enter. The land will pass from fathers to sons. And then five women walk up to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting and stand in front of Moses, Eleazar the priest, the chiefs and the entire community. Their names are Mahlah, Noa, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah. Their father, Zelophehad, had no sons.
screen: `A RULE THAT LEAVES YOU OUT.` → `FIVE WOMEN AT THE TENT.` → `THEIR FATHER HAD NO SONS.`

segments.voice: Here's what they say, in paraphrase. Our father died in the wilderness. He wasn't part of Korach's rebellion; he died in his own sin. And he had no sons. Why should our father's name disappear from his family just because he had no son? Give us a holding among our father's brothers. Notice how carefully they argue. They aren't asking for themselves first; they're asking that their father's name not be erased. They head off the obvious objection: he wasn't a rebel. And they make the request in public, before every authority at once. Moses doesn't answer. He brings their case before God. And God says, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "The daughters of Zelophehad speak right." Give them their father's inheritance. Then something bigger happens. The answer becomes a law for everyone: if a man dies without a son, his inheritance passes to his daughter. Five women standing at a tent changed the law for every family after them. The rabbis admired them enormously. The Talmud calls them wise, skilled at reading the law, and righteous, and says they chose their moment carefully, speaking when the subject of inheritance was already on the table. Some sages added that this passage of the Torah was meant to be written through them all along, as if God had been waiting for someone to ask. The daughters' names appear several times in the Bible, and they aren't always listed in the same order. One teaching reads that as a sign that all five were equal.
screen: `DON'T LET OUR FATHER'S NAME DISAPPEAR.` · `MOSES BRINGS IT BEFORE GOD.` · `THE DAUGHTERS SPEAK RIGHT.` · `ONE QUESTION, A LAW FOR ALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask for what's fair. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing in your life that feels unfair and that you've only complained about privately. A workload, a family arrangement, a policy. Now imagine standing at the tent like the five sisters. How would you put it, calmly and clearly? Who would you ask, and when would be the right moment? Find the first sentence, the one that names what's fair without attacking anyone. Hold it gently until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Pinchas. The portion where five sisters ask to inherit, and God tells Moses: the daughters of Zelophehad speak right.
Your line: the daughters speak right. Today, make one fair request out loud, to the person who can actually say yes. Day four hundred sixty-seven.

468.title: Pinchas: a shepherd for the flock (Numbers 27:15–17)
468.hook: Moses asks for a successor so the people won't be sheep without a shepherd
468.howItsDone: Moses' request for a successor is read in the portion of Pinchas in summer, and the phrase 'sheep without a shepherd' is often quoted in Jewish teaching about leadership and responsibility.

segments.voice: Yesterday, five sisters stood at the Tent of Meeting and asked to inherit, and God said the daughters speak right. Your line was the daughters speak right. Did you make a fair request out loud? Day four hundred sixty-eight.

A doctor's office, and the news no one wants to hear. How long? What can I do? Is there anything else? Those would be fair first questions. Right after the five sisters' case, God tells Moses to climb a mountain and look out at the land he will not enter, because soon he will die, like Aaron. It's hard news after so many years of leading. And the first words out of his mouth aren't about himself at all.
screen: `THE NEWS NO ONE WANTS.` → `CLIMB THE MOUNTAIN AND LOOK.` → `HIS FIRST WORDS AREN'T ABOUT HIM.`

segments.voice: Moses answers, in paraphrase: let the Lord, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint someone over the community, someone who will go out before them and come in before them, who will lead them out and bring them in, and then, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, "that the congregation of the LORD be not as sheep which have no shepherd." No protest. No bargaining for more time, not here. His first worry is the people after him. Look at the name he uses for God: the God of the spirits of all flesh. Rashi hears a request inside it. You know, Moses is saying, that every person's mind is different. Give them a leader who can bear with each one of them as they are. Moses had spent his years of leading learning exactly that. And notice the picture of a leader he asks for: one who goes out before them and comes in before them. Not one who sends people ahead, but one who walks first. Moses had been a shepherd before he was a prophet; he'd tended his father-in-law's flock in the wilderness when God first called him. He knew what happens to sheep with nobody in front. The midrash adds a human touch. It says Moses may have hoped one of his own sons would take over. Instead God chose Joshua, who had served Moses faithfully, and stayed close to the tent, for years. Moses didn't argue. The question he asked, before anything about himself, is one that parents, teachers and founders come to face too: who comes next?
screen: `HIS FIRST WORRY: THE PEOPLE AFTER HIM.` · `GOD OF THE SPIRITS OF ALL FLESH.` · `ONE WHO GOES OUT BEFORE THEM.` · `NOT HIS SONS, BUT JOSHUA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: prepare someone to follow you. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you do that matters to others: a job, a family role, a skill, a group you hold together. If you stepped away tomorrow, who would carry it? Picture that person. What's one thing you know that they don't yet? A recipe, where the spare key is kept, a way of handling a hard customer, a family story. Decide on one thing you could teach or write down for them this week. Breathe with it until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Pinchas. The portion where Moses, told he will die, first asks for a shepherd so the people won't be sheep without one.
Your line: who comes next. Today, teach one small thing you know to someone who might need it after you. Day four hundred sixty-eight.

469.title: Pinchas: some of thy honor (Numbers 27:18–23)
469.hook: Moses lays hands on Joshua and puts "of thy honor upon him"
469.howItsDone: Rabbinic ordination is still called semikhah, the word for Moses laying his hands on Joshua, and this passage is read each summer in the portion of Pinchas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, told he would die, Moses first asked for a shepherd so the people wouldn't be sheep without one. Your line was who comes next. What did you teach someone? Day four hundred sixty-nine.

The new manager starts on Monday. The old one can do two things. She can hand over the keys and the files and disappear. Or she can walk the new person around the office, introduce him to everyone by name, and say, in front of the whole team, I trust him. Same job. Very different start. God answers Moses' request: take Joshua, son of Nun, a man with spirit in him. And then come instructions about exactly how to hand over, in public, with his own hands.
screen: `THE NEW MANAGER STARTS MONDAY.` → `KEYS, OR A WALK AROUND THE OFFICE.` → `TAKE JOSHUA, SON OF NUN.`

segments.voice: Here's the instruction, in paraphrase. Take Joshua, lay your hand on him, stand him before Eleazar the priest and the whole community, and commission him in their sight. Then, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "thou shalt put of thy honour upon him," so that the whole community will listen to him. Of thy honor. Some of it. The Talmud noticed that word. Some, not all. The elders of that generation said, in paraphrase, Moses' face was like the sun, and Joshua's face like the moon. A real light, but a reflected one. The rabbis didn't say that to belittle Joshua. They said it to describe how leadership passes: the new leader shines, but in the beginning, partly with borrowed light. Then a small detail in the last verse. God told Moses to lay his hand on Joshua, singular. When Moses does it, the Torah says he laid his hands, plural. Rashi says Moses did more than he was asked, generously, with both hands, filling Joshua up the way you'd fill a vessel to overflowing. No jealousy, no holding back. That gesture has a name in Hebrew: semikhah, leaning or laying on of hands. Centuries later, the word semikhah came to mean rabbinic ordination, and it's still used today when a teacher authorizes a student to teach. So every time a rabbi receives semikhah, the word carries this moment: an old leader, about to step aside, putting both hands on the next one, in front of everyone.
screen: `COMMISSION HIM IN THEIR SIGHT.` · `OF THY HONOR: SUN AND MOON.` · `ONE HAND ASKED, TWO HANDS GIVEN.` · `SEMIKHAH: HANDS ON THE NEXT ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: share your standing with a newcomer. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone new in a place where you belong: a new coworker, a new member of your congregation or team, a new neighbor, a cousin's new partner. Picture them standing a little at the edge. What would it look like to lend them some of your honor? An introduction, a public word of trust, a seat next to you. Choose one small way. Breathe with it until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Pinchas. The portion where Moses lays both hands on Joshua. And this week: the true word, Mah Tovu, a people dwelling alone, a broken letter of peace, five sisters, a shepherd, and now the hands.
Your line: hands on the next one. Today, introduce someone newer than you to someone who matters, and say one good thing about them out loud. Day four hundred sixty-nine.
